summary:
SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months in 102 infrared bands, which is far more than experts alone can search. SPHEREx Blink turns this free but hard-to-use data into something anyone can explore.

SPHEREx Blink is a public web tool that lets anyone spot moving and changing objects in the sky using images taken by the Spherex, with no coding or astronomy software needed.

Users type a known object name or sky coordinates, and the tool plays every SPHEREx image of that spot in time order, like a flip-book, so anything that moved or changed brightness stands out. Difference and IR colour modes make faint and cold objects easier to see, and users can choose the detector, wavelength band and field of view. Clicking any dot runs “Is it new?”: the object is checked against Gaia, SIMBAD and known asteroids, its measured motion is compared with the catalogue, and the result is explained in plain language. Spectrum, motion and brightness charts, plus a sky map, add context. Every view is a shareable link that can be embedded in other sites.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SPHEREx Blink is a free web tool that makes NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky survey easy for anyone to explore. Users type an object name (like "WISE 0855") or sky coordinates. The tool plays every SPHEREx image of that spot in time order, one frame per six-month survey pass, so anything that moved or changed brightness jumps out. It's the same "blink" method that found Pluto.

There are three display modes. Blink flips through the passes. Difference shows where an object was (blue) and where it is now (red). IR colour maps three infrared bands to red, green and blue, so cold brown dwarfs look red. Users can pick the detector, wavelength band, zoom and brightness. Overlays mark known stars, asteroids and bad pixels.

Clicking any dot runs "Is it new?". It checks the object against Gaia DR3, SIMBAD and the SkyBoT asteroid service, compares its measured motion with the catalogue, and explains the verdict in plain language. Spectrum, motion and brightness charts and an Aladin Lite sky map add context. Every view is a shareable link, and an embed mode lets other sites include the viewer.

HOW IT WORKS

The frontend uses React and Vite, with a canvas player, Recharts and Aladin Lite. The backend is Python FastAPI with Astropy, Astroquery, PyVO, Reproject, NumPy, SciPy and Pillow. It queries NASA/IPAC's IRSA archive (DR1 and QR3 releases) and reads only the small pixel box it needs from IRSA's public cloud storage, falling back to the cutout service if needed. It then stacks exposures per pass and renders the frames. Slow requests run as background jobs with progress shown on the page, and results are cached. We tested on the challenge targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

SPHEREx images over a billion objects, far more than experts can inspect, and its public data is hard to use without programming. SPHEREx Blink removes that barrier. Citizen scientists can hunt for brown dwarfs, comets and nearby stars from a browser, teachers get a lesson built on live NASA data, and researchers get an instant quick look. Our goal is to turn SPHEREx into a public discovery engine.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Most viewers stop at the image. Ours answers the question users actually have, "Has anyone found this before?", with real catalogue checks and plain-language explanations. IR colour puts SPHEREx's many wavelengths to work, and the interface is built around a glowing dome of the SPHEREx all-sky map.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

  • Non-experts first: plain words, sensible defaults and ready-made starting targets.
  • Honesty: the verdict is a guide backed by catalogue data, not a claim of discovery.
  • New data: releases are a setting, so updates need no code changes.
  • Speed and cost: small pixel reads, caching and background jobs.
  • Accessibility: keyboard controls, screen-reader labels, phone layouts and colour-blind-friendly orange/blue charts.
